Apollo 16 Mission Report (MSC-07230), Table 3-1 and maneuver summary, NTRS 19720026127
Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A, 1972-04-16 17:54:00 UTC (12:54 p.m. EST). Saturn V lifts Young, Mattingly and Duke on the first mission to the lunar highlands.
S-IVB second burn at GET 2:33:37 (1972-04-16 20:27 UTC), 341.9 seconds, 10,389.6 ft/s (3,167 m/s).
SPS burn at GET 30:39:01 (1972-04-18 00:33 UTC), 2.0 s and 12.5 ft/s (3.8 m/s), the only translunar correction.
1972-04-19 20:22 UTC, GET 74:28:28. A 374.9-second SPS burn, 2,802 ft/s (854 m/s), captures Casper and Orion into a 170.3 x 58.1 mile orbit; descent orbit insertion follows at GET 78:33:45.
1972-04-21 02:11 UTC, GET 104:17:25. A 734-second descent burn ends at GET 104:29:35 in the Descartes highlands.
1972-04-24 01:25 UTC, GET 175:31:48. A 427.7-second ascent burn after three EVAs; docking with Casper at GET 177:41:18.
1972-04-25 02:15 UTC, GET 200:21:33. A 162.3-second SPS burn, 3,370.9 ft/s (1,027 m/s), follows the subsatellite launch at GET 196:02:09.
8.0-second RCS correction at GET 214:35:03 (1972-04-25 16:29 UTC), 3.4 ft/s; a second 3.2-second trim follows at GET 262:37:21.
Final entry-corridor trim at GET 262:37:21 (1972-04-27 16:31 UTC), 1.4 ft/s.
1972-04-27 19:45 UTC, GET 265:51:05. Apollo 16 lands after 11 days 1 h 51 min.
First Moon landing in the lunar highlands — Descartes; John Young's "lunar Grand Prix"

Apollo 16 went to the lunar highlands to sample ancient volcanoes and found there had never been any. Geologists were sure the pale, rugged Descartes region was volcanic; nearly every rock Young and Duke brought back was breccia — rubble welded together by impacts — and none was volcanic. Being wrong was the payoff: the Moon's bright highlands turned out to be a record of a young solar system under relentless bombardment, not eruption. It is a clean example of how exploration actually earns its keep — you go to confirm what you already think you know, and the place tells you something better.

The fifth crewed Moon landing and the first to a non-mare highland site. Geologists had expected Descartes to be volcanic; Apollo 16 disproved this — nearly every rock returned was breccia (impact-shattered debris), and none was volcanic, reshaping understanding of the lunar highlands as products of catastrophic impacts rather than ancient volcanism. Young and Duke completed three LRV-supported EVAs totalling 20 h 14 m, traversed 26.7 km, and returned 95.7 kg of samples (the heaviest Apollo haul to that date). Young's "lunar Grand Prix" — a televised speed test of the LRV — peaked at ~17 km/h. At the end of the third moonwalk Duke fell backwards onto his PLSS backpack during a high-jump attempt. Charlie Duke's family photo + the "Far-UV Camera/Spectrograph" — the first astronomical observatory operated from the surface of another world — both ended up at the landing site. Mattingly, originally on Apollo 13 (replaced before launch over German measles concerns), finally got to fly to the Moon.
Saturn V (AS-511) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1972-04-16 17:54 UTC.
Pre-descent: a backup SPS gimbal oscillation forced a 6-hour landing-vs-abort engineering review in real time. Landing ultimately approved.
Orion lands at Descartes Highlands 1972-04-21 02:23 UTC — first highland (non-mare) landing.
EVA-1: ALSEP deployment + LRV deployment + first scientific traverse of the lunar highlands.
EVA-2: Young's televised LRV speed test ("lunar Grand Prix") — peak speed ~17 km/h. Geology traverse up Stone Mountain.
EVA-3: First astronomical observatory deployed on the surface of another world (NRL UV camera-spectrograph).
Orion lifts off after 71 h 02 m on surface. 95.7 kg samples returned — heaviest Apollo haul to that date.
CM splashed down in Central Pacific 1972-04-27 19:45 UTC. Recovery by USS Ticonderoga.
